newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-OLAZABAL AND PALMER IN ROUSING RETURN TO MASTERS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-OLAZABAL AND PALMER IN ROUSING RETURN TO MASTERS.

text.p: Nick Faldo and Greg Norman may dream of another Masters Sunday with the title on the line, but two extraordinary former champions are just happy to be back once again to beautiful Augusta National.

Not long ago neither Jose Maria Olazabal and Arnold Palmer could be confident of ever playing another Masters, but both are here for the season's first major championship, eager to tee it up in Thursday's opening round.
Olazabal, the 1994 champion, spent 18 months wondering whether he would spend the rest of his life in a wheelchair. Pain in his feet ruined him for golf and much of anything else.
"I'm just happy to be here," said the 31-year-old Olazabal. "I think that should be very obvious to anybody. I've been through a terrible period of time, but right now I'm feeling much better."

Olazabal was diagnosed at first with rheumatoid arthritis in his feet. He made no progress until a German homeopathic specialist diagnosed the cause as a lower back hernia. Vitamin injections and an exercise regimen eased the pain and enabled him to return to golf.
"I never gave up," said Olazabal. "I thought about it, but I never gave up."
Olazabal said he could not pinpoint the blackest day of his ordeal, saying simply: "When you cannot walk at all, I think that's the lowest you can get. Especially when you're 31."

The Spaniard made a stunning return, finishing tied for 12th to start this European tour season in Dubai and tied for fourth two weeks later in the Portuguese Open. He thrilled golf fans the world over last month by winning the Turespana Masters in the Canary Islands.
"That was a special moment, obviously," said Olazabal. "I don't think you've seen me cry on the golf course many times before. I did that day."

Palmer, diagnosed with prostate cancer in January, had surgery five days later. The dynamic Palmer, who thrust golf into prominence at the blossoming of the television age, is elated to be back and competing in his 43rd successive Masters.
"I felt very good and walked all the way through 18 holes and then hit some balls at the range," said Palmer, 67, who piloted his own particularly-fast Cessna jet to Augusta. "I'm happy to be here.
"It's sort of like looking down on the grass rather than up at it," Palmer said, joking about his mortality.

Palmer, a four-time Masters winner, enjoyed a flashback during his practice round Tuesday with Tom Watson, Fuzzy Zoeller and amateur Spider Miller when he hit a sweet eight iron into the troublesome par-three 12th and made a birdie two.

"It reminded me of the playoff with Gary Player and Dow Finsterwald in '62 when I hit a little eight iron and made two and I did the same today," he said recalling his triumph in the Masters' first three-way playoff.
Faldo, whose brilliant final-round 67 last year enabled him to overtake Norman, relishes another crack at proving himself under fire against the 86-man field.
"You always wonder when your next win will be and you question more if you've still got another major in you," said Faldo, who has triple crowns in the Masters and British Open.
"That was the nicest feeling for me at the end of the day when I left last year. 'Wow, I've still got it in me.' To win another one was a great feeling."

Faldo, hoping to become the first player to win back to back Masters twice, had the groundskeeper at his Florida home course of Lake Nona shave down the greens to approximate the speed of Augusta National's vaunted putting surfaces.
He sounded charged up yet again by the lure of Augusta.

"There's a very electric atmosphere out there. This is the Masters. The whole picture of it," Faldo said. "It's got the beauty, it's got the colour, the sound. You've got the breeze. Everything put together makes this place something special."
Norman, his faith in himself restored by cable television motivator Tony Robbins, said Sweden's Jesper Parnevik asked him last week about playing Augusta National for the first time.

"You're going to experience something you never experienced before," he said. "You're going to go down Magnolia Lane, you're going to get nervous butterflies in your stomach. Just accept the fact that it is a tough golf course to play."

There are a host of hot contenders for the title, including Australian Steve Elkington, the PGA Tour's leading money winner, and those shooting for their first major such as Briton Colin Montgomerie and Americans Phil Mickelson, Davis Love III and 21- year-old star Tiger Woods.
Palmer praised the Masters for preserving golf tradition.

"I think back over the years since I first came here, and what has transpired in those 42 years is just magnificent. To still be coming here and to see the expansion and the integrity and the quality of the game is very, very pleasing to me.
"The Masters is an example of how something can expand and become far more worldly than it was 42 years ago and still be good and still present a wonderful picture.
"I just hope that when Tiger Woods has been here 42 years, that he can sit here and say the same thing to people coming on behind him."
